programme: Twelve-week Ledger API, Platform & Reliability Engineering

assumptions.api_experience: Assume no current API-building experience and no reliable recall of FastAPI; teach HTTP and API design first, then build the app step by step.
assumptions.python_experience: Do not schedule Python fundamentals. Assume the learner knows Python and can read/write ordinary application code; only cover environment and dependency setup as needed for the project.
assumptions.platform_experience: Confirmed 25 Nov 2026: the learner does not use Docker, Kubernetes or AWS at work, so the Docker, Kubernetes and AWS sessions keep their full length. AWS foundations (D49) may be shortened if IAM, VPC and EC2 prove familiar.
assumptions.container_runtime: Reuse existing Colima Docker runtime; do not install Docker Desktop.
assumptions.optional_extensions: Selected sessions include an optional 15-minute stretch; never required.
assumptions.project_approach: Start with the request/response model and endpoint contract before implementing routes. Avoid large code dumps; build one endpoint at a time and explain each decision.
assumptions.project_domain: Build a simulated double-entry ledger API, not a generic task manager. No real funds or payment rails.
assumptions.database: Use PostgreSQL for the main application; money is stored as BIGINT minor units. SQLite is not part of the application architecture.
assumptions.git_and_publishing: Commit and push from D2. A private repository is recommended for work-in-progress code. CI starts at D22 and image publishing at D30.
assumptions.observability: Prometheus and Grafana run in a Docker Compose profile and are core, with Locust generating traffic. Grafana-managed alerts use Prometheus recording rules. Structured stdout logs are core. Loki/Alloy and OpenTelemetry/Jaeger are optional.
assumptions.cloud: The AWS exercise is temporary and cost-controlled and uses Session Manager instead of inbound SSH. Never assume a free tier; estimate costs before apply, set a budget alert first, and verify destroy.
assumptions.interview_practice: DSA is a separate optional side track of three 30-minute sessions per week; it does not displace the 60-minute core session. Reduce to two 15-minute sessions in demanding weeks.
assumptions.flex_sessions: Five flex sessions sit on holidays (25 Dec, 1 Jan, 14 Jan, 15 Jan, 26 Jan). If behind, use them for catch-up; if on schedule, rest or do optional work. Weeks 11-12 independent sessions are the second buffer.

cadence.first_week_exception: Start Tuesday 24 November 2026; Week 1 has five study sessions (Tuesday–Saturday). Sundays remain review/rest days.

days.title: API lab setup and first FastAPI process
days.objective: Verify the existing Colima/Docker setup without changing it; check Python/Git versions; create the reliability-lab-api folder and virtual environment; install FastAPI; create a minimal app and run it locally.
days.deliverable: A minimal FastAPI application running locally, a clean project folder, .venv excluded from Git, and /docs opening in the browser.
days.notes: Completed and verified interactively. Colima started successfully; Docker uses the colima context and the Docker CLI discovers the Homebrew Compose plugin. Python 3.14.2 and Git 2.56.1 available. Created reliability-lab-api with an active .venv, .gitignore excluding .venv and Python cache files, and installed FastAPI 0.165.0 (fastapi[standard]). Created main.py with GET / returning {"message":"Hello, world!"}. FastAPI dev server started at http://127.0.0.1:8000; terminal logs confirm GET /, /docs, and /openapi.json returned HTTP 200. favicon.ico 404 is harmless.

check Python/Git versions
create the reliability-lab-api folder and virtual environment
install FastAPI
create a minimal app and run it locally.

days.title: HTTP anatomy, URLs and headers
days.objective: Understand client/server request and response anatomy using your own D1 app: label the method, URL parts (scheme, host, port, path, query), headers, body and status line with curl -v. In the build block, commit the D1 project and push it to GitHub.
days.deliverable: A labelled request/response example for GET /accounts and POST /transfers (including Content-Type and Idempotency-Key headers), and the D1 project committed and pushed to a GitHub repository.
days.notes: Completed and verified interactively. Reviewed HTTP client/server request-response flow; identified request lines, URL components, headers, blank-line separation, optional bodies, response status line, response headers and JSON body. Inspected the local FastAPI GET / exchange with curl -v: request GET / HTTP/1.1, Host 127.0.0.1:8000, User-Agent curl/8.7.1, Accept */*, response HTTP/1.1 200 OK, server uvicorn, content-type application/json, and JSON body {"message":"Hello, World!"}. Distinguished path parameters, query parameters, HTTP headers and JSON request bodies using Ledger API examples. Initialized local Git repository, retained local .gitignore and main.py, synchronized the pre-existing GitHub history, excluded .venv and __pycache__, added basic .env/key and macOS ignore rules, configured existing Ed25519 SSH key and GitHub SSH authentication, switched origin to SSH, and successfully pushed main. Remote main advanced to merge commit c73164a; upstream tracking set to origin/main.
tasks: Label request line, URL components, headers, body and response fields on a sample exchange
Use curl -v against the local D1 app and read the request and response headers
Compare path parameters, query parameters, headers and JSON bodies
Commit the D1 project (without .venv) and push it to GitHub; a private repository is recommended for work-in-progress code

days.title: HTTP methods, retries and idempotency
days.objective: Map GET and POST to account and transfer operations; learn safe versus idempotent methods; understand why a transfer POST needs an application-level idempotency key and why posted ledger entries are never edited or deleted.
days.deliverable: A method-to-action table for the Ledger API and a short note on safe retries and on why PATCH and DELETE are not offered for posted transfers.
days.extension_task: Write the two-sentence explanation of idempotency you would give a teammate.
days.notes: Completed and verified interactively. Mapped GET /accounts, GET /accounts/{account_id}, GET /transfers/{transfer_id}, and POST /transfers to their purposes and safe/idempotent semantics. Distinguished safe methods from idempotent methods: safe operations do not intend to change application state; idempotent operations have the same intended effect when repeated, even if responses differ. Reviewed GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE; understood that PATCH may be designed idempotently or non-idempotently and POST is appropriate for creating a transfer as a new business transaction rather than directly updating a balance. Explained timeout ambiguity and why retrying POST without protection can create duplicate transfers. Defined project retry rules: same key and same payload returns original result; same key and different payload returns 409 Conflict; a genuinely new operation gets a new key. Understood need for a database uniqueness constraint to handle concurrent requests racing to claim the same key. Reviewed immutable debit/credit ledger entries and compensating transactions for corrections. Final checkpoint answers correct.
tasks: Map GET /accounts, GET /accounts/{id}, GET /transfers/{id} and POST /transfers to HTTP methods
Distinguish safe methods from idempotent methods
Explain what happens when a client retries POST /transfers after a timeout, with and without an idempotency key
Explain why corrections are made with compensating entries instead of edits

days.title: Status codes and error design
days.objective: Review the status-code groups and choose codes for validation failure, unknown account, insufficient funds, conflicting idempotency key and unexpected failure; define one consistent JSON error shape (RFC 9457 problem details is a good model).
days.deliverable: A status-code decision table and one documented error-response shape for the Ledger API.

resources.name: RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs

tasks: Review 2xx, 4xx and 5xx groups and the difference between 400, 404, 409 and 422
Choose a status code for each Ledger API failure case
Define the error body shape (RFC 9457 is optional but recommended)
List what must never appear in an error body: SQL, stack traces, secrets, internal identifiers

days.title: Ledger API resource design and contract
days.objective: Design the Account, Transfer and LedgerEntry resources and write the API contract before implementing any route: methods, paths, example requests and responses, status codes and idempotency behaviour.
days.deliverable: ledger-api-contract.md with every endpoint, example request and response, status codes and error shape.
days.extension_task: Review the contract and remove any endpoint or field that is not necessary for the learning project.
tasks: Define Account, Transfer and LedgerEntry fields; amounts are integer minor units (BIGINT in PostgreSQL)
Design POST /accounts, GET /accounts and GET /accounts/{account_id}
Design GET /accounts/{account_id}/entries with limit/offset pagination
Design POST /transfers (Idempotency-Key header required) and GET /transfers/{transfer_id}
List every error case with its status code and response shape

days.deliverable: Two account endpoints with predictable success, empty-list, not-found and invalid-ID behaviour.
days.extension_task: Explain the difference between a route path and the value supplied for a path parameter.

days.objective: Add GET /accounts/{account_id}/entries over an in-memory entry list with limit and offset query parameters, sensible defaults, enforced maximums and stable ordering.
days.deliverable: An entry-history endpoint with bounded pagination and documented examples.
days.extension_task: Test boundary values for limit and offset and document what the API returns.

days.title: Request models, validation and POST /accounts (in-memory)
days.objective: Create the AccountCreate and TransferCreate request models; validate name, currency code and positive integer amounts; implement POST /accounts against the in-memory list and read FastAPI validation errors.
days.deliverable: POST /accounts returns 201 for valid input and a clear 422 for invalid input; TransferCreate is defined and validated.
days.extension_task: Add a maximum length for the account name and test both boundaries.

Implement POST /accounts in memory and return 201

days.title: Response models and consistent errors
days.objective: Separate input, storage and output shapes; create AccountRead, LedgerEntryRead and TransferRead response models; apply the single error shape from D4 to 404, 409 and 422 responses; move the routes into an APIRouter module.
days.deliverable: Endpoints use explicit response models and one consistent error body; the generated OpenAPI schemas look right.
days.extension_task: Show with a curl example that internal-only fields are never returned.

days.title: Containers from first principles and your first PostgreSQL container

days.title: SQL and relational modelling for the ledger
days.objective: Learn tables, keys, constraints and indexes with short interactive SQL practice, then write the ledger schema by hand in SQL on your PostgreSQL container: accounts, transfers, ledger_entries and idempotency_records.
days.deliverable: A schema.sql with keys, foreign keys, unique and CHECK constraints and BIGINT money columns, plus queries for an account balance and an account history.

days.objective: Model Account, Transfer, LedgerEntry and IdempotencyRecord in SQLModel on top of SQLAlchemy; use BigInteger for money, unique, foreign-key and CHECK constraints; create the tables in a disposable database (temporary create_all) and compare with your hand-written schema.

days.title: Atomic transfers and double-entry posting
days.objective: Implement POST /transfers in one database transaction: validate accounts and currency, lock both account rows in a consistent order, check funds, insert the transfer and balanced debit/credit entries, update both balances and commit; force a failure and prove everything rolls back.

days.extension_task: Add a CHECK constraint or a test that makes a negative balance impossible.

days.title: Idempotency keys
days.objective: Persist the Idempotency-Key and a fingerprint of the request; return the original result for an identical retry and a conflict for a different payload using the same key; rely on a unique constraint, not on an application-level check alone.
days.deliverable: Evidence that repeated identical requests create one transfer and that a changed payload with the same key returns 409.

migration_note: Earlier revisions (kept for history): Revised on 2026-11-23 after learner clarified that Python fundamentals are not needed. Rebased on 2026-11-23 for a Tuesday 2026-11-24 start; Sundays remain review/rest days; Week 1 is a five-session kickoff; Weeks 2-12 contain six sessions. Revised on 2026-11-24 after external review: changed generic Task API to a simulated double-entry Ledger API; replaced SQLite with PostgreSQL; added idempotency, atomic transfers, concurrency, Alembic, CI/CD, Terraform, a cost-controlled AWS EC2 deployment, Linux troubleshooting and SLO burn-rate alerts. Revised on 2026-11-25 (schema_version 3): removed duplicated in-memory work and merged HTTP basics; moved the first Docker/PostgreSQL container to D11; pushed code from D2 and moved CI to D22 and GHCR publishing to D30; replaced the Task-API-era extension tasks; added a Locust traffic generator, a single Compose-based observability stack, Grafana-managed burn-rate alerts with a local alert sink, BIGINT money columns, Session Manager instead of SSH, five holiday flex sessions (session_type 'flex') and a 3x30-minute optional DSA track. Preserved all 71 dates, the review cadence and D1 completion evidence.
lab_method: Use a short free browser lab for Docker (D11) and Kubernetes (D31, D32) as a supplement and reproduce everything locally through Colima and k3d. Browser labs are disposable; the repository is the source of truth.
browser_lab_safety: Do not enter production credentials, AWS keys, tokens or personal data into public labs. Use fake database passwords in local examples.
observability_signals: core metrics: Prometheus request/latency/transfer metrics and PromQL, with Locust traffic
core dashboards/alerts: Grafana dashboard and Grafana-managed multi-window burn-rate alerts on Prometheus recording rules, delivered to a local alert sink
core logs: structured application stdout and Docker/Kubernetes/cloud log inspection
optional log aggregation: Grafana Alloy and Loki
aws_lab_safety: AWS resources can incur charges and free-tier eligibility is not guaranteed. Create a budget alert first, review the pricing calculator, avoid NAT gateways/load balancers/managed Kubernetes/RDS, use Session Manager instead of inbound SSH, run terraform destroy and verify cleanup. Never paste credentials into chat or commit secrets, tfvars or Terraform state.

interview_track.name: Python DSA interview practice
interview_track.cadence: Three optional 30-minute sessions per week, outside the 60-minute core curriculum: one timed attempt, one review, one re-solve
interview_track.approach: Use Python for problem solving; this is not a Python syntax course. State complexity, compare an alternative and record one mistake or pattern per problem. Reduce to two 15-minute sessions in demanding weeks.
